title: What a default says
bodyMd:
When employers began enrolling new staff in workplace pension schemes automatically, leaving them free to opt out, participation rose sharply. In one group of firms, the share of new employees contributing within their first year rose from under half to over ninety per cent. Economists had long assumed that a worker who wanted to save would sign up and a worker who did not would not, so that the choice of default should change little. The evidence suggested instead that many workers simply stay wherever they are placed.

That finding has been read in two quite different ways. On the first reading, the default works through inertia: many workers would like to save but put off the paperwork, so automatic enrolment helps them do what they already intended. On the second, the default works because workers take it as advice: an employer that enrols them at a contribution rate of three per cent appears to be recommending three per cent.

The two readings agree that participation rises, but they predict different things for workers who were always going to join. If inertia is the whole story, a default should change nothing for them: they would have signed up and chosen their own rate anyway, and automatic enrolment merely spares them a form. If the default is read as advice, some of them will treat the suggested figure as the right one and contribute less than they otherwise would have. Several studies have found exactly this second pattern: after automatic enrolment was introduced at a low default rate, the average contribution among workers of the kind who had previously joined voluntarily fell.

None of this makes automatic enrolment a mistake. It does mean that the default rate is not a neutral starting point but a message, and that a scheme judged only by how many people it enrols may be quietly lowering how much they save.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage, with no figure or table, about automatic enrolment in workplace pensions. Participation rose from under half to over ninety per cent when enrolment became automatic. Two readings are described: inertia, where workers who meant to save are spared the paperwork; and advice, where workers take the default contribution rate as a recommendation. The readings differ on workers who would have joined anyway: under inertia alone nothing changes for them, under advice some lower their contributions to the default. Studies found the second pattern. The author concludes automatic enrolment is not a mistake but the default rate is a message, and judging a scheme only by enrolment may hide lower saving.
